name: InfoDeepSeek: Benchmarking Agentic Information Seeking for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.15872 (cs.IR; cs.CL), submitted 21 May 2025, v2 23 May 2025. Also under review (an OpenReview forum exists at openreview.net/forum?id=snm8tq7sdI). No peer-reviewed proceedings venue confirmed as of mid-2026. DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2505.15872.

code_url: https://github.com/YunjiaXi/InfoDeepSeek (the InfoSeekAgents agentic-RAG harness + eval scripts; CC BY-NC 4.0). Dataset on HuggingFace: https://huggingface.co/datasets/yoga334/InfoDeekSeek (also data/InfoDeepSeek_v1.json in the repo). Project page: https://infodeepseek.github.io/
maintained_repo_url: https://github.com/YunjiaXi/InfoDeepSeek (project page https://infodeepseek.github.io/). The authors do not maintain a public live leaderboard; the repo (5 commits, ~18 stars as of mid-2026) and the HuggingFace dataset (InfoDeepSeek_v1, 245 queries) are the canonical sources. The work is listed in third-party trackers such as github.com/qhjqhj00/awesome-agentic-search.
task_domain: web / QA / decision-making: a benchmark for agentic information seeking (Agentic RAG) in open, dynamic real-world web environments. Factual open-domain QA requiring multi-turn web search and browsing, planning, disambiguation, and cross-lingual retrieval; touches tool-use (search engines, browser, time utilities) and multi-step decision-making.
problem_setting: Interactive, single-agent, test-time online setting in the live open web (no fixed corpus). Given a query q, an Agentic RAG agent iteratively plans, acts (search engine / Selenium browser / time tool / terminate), observes, and reflects for up to T steps (default T=5) to acquire an evidence set C (size n_q, capped at n=5) from the real web, then generates an answer. The environment is dynamic (web content is volatile and multi-source), so ground-truth retrieval documents cannot be pre-fixed; only ground-truth answers and a human-annotated standard set of supporting source webpages S_q are recorded. No training/supervision is provided to the agent: the benchmark evaluates off-the-shelf LLMs zero-shot under a unified plan-reflect-act framework. Questions are deliberately filtered so neither GPT-4o nor DeepSeek-R1 can solve them with a single-turn web search, forcing genuine multi-round agentic behavior. Dataset: 245 validated queries, each carrying >=2 of six difficulty attributes, 14 domains, 19 predominant languages, all provided in both English and Chinese.
what_is_retrieved: docs (live web content): web search results / snippets / page titles and full webpage contents fetched from real search engines (Google, Bing, Yahoo, DuckDuckGo) and a Selenium browser. The agent distills these into an ordered evidence set C of up to n=5 webpages (URL + extracted relevant content). It is open-web documents/evidence, not demos/cases/tools/skills.
retrieval_grounding: STATIC external corpus in the loose sense of querying the open, live web (a dynamic external information source the agent does NOT write to). It is NOT a growing/episodic agent memory: the agent has a per-query working memory (its own trajectory) used for planning, but retrieval targets the external web, and nothing is persisted back into a retrievable store across queries. Best described as retrieval over a dynamic external corpus (the live web) rather than over a fixed offline KB or an agent-written memory.
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Completeness-and-precision oriented with a variable-size, capped recommendation: the agent must recover the complete minimal set of supporting sources needed to answer (multi-hop questions need multiple sources; annotated |S_q| typically 1-3). The agent dynamically chooses the evidence-set size n_q up to a cap n=5 and ranks evidence by importance. Evaluation rewards both having sufficient top-k evidence (IA@k) and keeping the set compact (Information Compactness penalizes over-retrieval), i.e., a precision-driven variable-size objective rather than a fixed top-k ranking.
retrieval_unit: document / webpage (and snippet): the retrievable observation is a web search result snippet, page title, or full webpage content; the curated evidence unit c_i is a webpage represented as (URL, query-relevant extracted content). Selection operates at both document-level and span-level.
index_source: Dynamic external corpus = the live, open web, queried online at test time through commercial/free search-engine APIs and a Selenium browser. There is no offline-induced index and no agent-written store; the 'index' is whatever the real-time search engine and the web return for each query, making it volatile and source-multiplicitous by design.
index_structure_topology: No constructed index structure: retrieval is delegated to external general-purpose search engines (Google/Bing/Yahoo/DuckDuckGo) whose internal indexes are opaque, plus direct Selenium browsing of live URLs. On the agent side the retrieved content is held as a flat, chronologically-appended trajectory memory (plans + actions + observations); the curated evidence set C is a flat importance-sorted list of <=5 webpages. No vector index, dependency graph, or hierarchical topology is built by the benchmark.
retriever_type: LLM-as-retriever orchestrating external search-engine tools: the LLM agent forms search keyword queries and decides which tool to call (search engine or browser); the actual lexical/semantic matching is performed by the black-box commercial search engines (BM25/dense hybrid internally, not controlled by the benchmark). For the augmentation stage, the LLM also acts as a relevance selector/ranker over retrieved content. So: hybrid = LLM-driven query formulation + tool/search-engine backend + LLM-based relevance selection.
retriever_learning_signal: none (off-the-shelf): neither the search engines nor the LLM agent are trained or fine-tuned for retrieval in this benchmark. All LLMs are evaluated zero-shot under a fixed unified plan-reflect-act prompt; query construction and evidence selection rely on the LLM's pretrained capabilities. The benchmark studies behavior, not a learned retriever; no contrastive/LM-feedback/preference/RL retrieval signal is introduced.
query_construction: LLM-generated search keywords conditioned on the query, current plan, observations, and trajectory memory. The agent decomposes complex queries into sub-problems during planning and issues per-step search keyword queries (the paper notes search keywords are strongly aligned with the input language; a language-aware prompt can force use of a predominant language). Thus queries are thought/plan-conditioned, decomposed sub-queries, not raw verbatim input.
query_granularity: step/state-level (iterative): a fresh search query is constructed at each of the up to T reasoning steps based on the evolving plan and prior observations, rather than a single one-shot task-level query at t=0. Initial planning happens at t=0 but retrieval queries are issued and refined per step.
when_to_retrieve: iterative / agent-initiated (active): the agent retrieves across multiple steps (up to T, default 5; ablated 1-20) and decides at each step whether to search/browse again or invoke the termination tool when it judges the gathered information sufficient. Retrieval is interleaved with planning and reflection; it is not one-shot.
retrieval_trigger_signal: Agent-initiated request driven by self-assessed sufficiency: at each step the LLM plans/reflects and either issues another search/browse action or calls the explicit termination tool once it deems the information sufficient (subject to the hard step cap T). The trigger is the agent's own reasoning ('call the tool for questions you are not sure about'; 'if you have sufficient information ... invoke the termination tool'), not a learned router, token-confidence, attention, or reflection-token mechanism.
reranking: Yes, LLM-based importance ranking in the augmentation stage: the agent consolidates retrieved content, merges duplicate-URL pieces, selects the <=n (=5) most relevant webpages, and sorts them by importance/contribution to answering the query (the first-ranked page contributes most). This is an LLM relevance-and-coverage reranker over raw observations, not a trained cross-encoder or RRF.
retrieved_context_refinement: Distillation + selection + dedup: the augmentation stage applies document-level and span-level selection, summarizes/extracts query-relevant content from each webpage, removes redundancy by merging identical-URL evidence, ranks by relevance/coverage/redundancy, and truncates to <=5 evidence items. Effectively a reason-in-documents distillation plus distractor-filtering/compression step performed by the LLM.
how_retrieved_used: prompt augmentation: the curated, importance-sorted evidence set C (and, for ACC, the full observation sequence O) is provided to the LLM in the generation stage to produce the final answer y_hat = Generate(q, C). The retrieved web evidence grounds the answer; there is no skill reuse, case adaptation, training signal, or latent-token injection.
planning_integration: Per-step interleaved retrieve-while-planning inside an iterative agent loop: initial plan at t=0, then a plan-act-reflect cycle (Plan -> Act with a tool -> Observe -> Reflect/replan) for up to T steps, followed by a separate augmentation (select-and-rank) stage and then generation. It is neither one-shot retrieve-then-plan nor tree-search/MCTS; retrieval and planning are tightly interleaved step by step, with explicit reflection on accumulated trajectory memory.
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: per-step within a rollout: retrieval (a search-engine or browser tool call) is woven into reasoning at the granularity of each planning step (up to T steps), with reflection between steps. Not per-token/per-sentence; closer to per-tool-call / per-reasoning-step interleaving.
retrieved_item_representation: Structured note per webpage: each evidence item is injected as a (URL, query-relevant extracted/summarized content) record, sorted by importance. It is distilled free-text web content with provenance (URL), not raw full pages, executable programs, latent tokens, or abstract strategies.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Raw/lightly-distilled factual web evidence: the unit is concrete document/webpage content (snippets and extracted spans relevant to the query), optionally summarized. It is reference evidence, not a distilled strategy, guideline/rule, reusable workflow, or procedural skill.
noise_robustness_mechanism: Built into the framework and measured by the benchmark: (1) the augmentation stage's relevance selection + summarization + dedup + importance ranking is the primary noise-filtering mechanism; (2) the planning prompt instructs the agent to verify truthfulness and cross-check; (3) the benchmark explicitly quantifies failure to filter noise via Effective Evidence Utilization (EEU) and Information Compactness (IC), and surfaces a 'retrieval interference' phenomenon (model answers correctly without retrieval but wrongly after noisy retrieval) with a defined interference-rate metric. No trained retriever-aware/distractor-aware SFT module; robustness relies on the LLM's in-context filtering, which the paper shows is weak (EEU mostly <1).
memory_type: episodic (per-query working memory only): the agent maintains a within-episode memory of all past plans, actions/queries, and observations (~4,000-char short-term memory) used for planning and reflection. There is no persistent skill-library, workflow, graph, or latent memory and no cross-query memory.
write_back: false: nothing is written to a persistent/retrievable store. The per-query trajectory memory is updated during an episode for planning/reflection but is discarded after the query; no cases/skills/experiences are saved for reuse on later queries.
online_growth: false: there is no retrievable store that grows during deployment. The external 'corpus' is the live web (changes independently of the agent, but the agent does not add to a controlled index), and the agent's episodic memory does not persist or accumulate across queries.
write_back_trigger: never: the benchmark/framework performs no write-back of experiences. Within an episode the working memory is appended every step (plans, actions, observations) purely as transient context for the next planning/reflection step, but this is not persisted as a learned memory after the query, so there is no success/failure/reflective write-back to a durable store.
failure_experience_usage: N/A / none: failed trajectories or wrong answers are not stored or retrieved as negative experiences. The paper analyzes failure phenomena (e.g., retrieval interference, fail cases for the unified prompting strategy) for scientific insight, but does not persist failures for contrastive or corrective retrieval.
memory_evolution_update: Append-only within an episode (transient): the per-query trajectory memory is appended with each new plan/action/observation and used for reflection; no dedup-merge, delta-update, refine-overwrite, forget-prune, or link-and-evolve of a persistent store occurs (the augmentation stage does merge identical-URL evidence, but that is one-shot evidence-set construction, not memory evolution).
retrieval_as_learned_policy: No: retrieval/search and evidence selection are driven by a fixed, prompted LLM policy (plan-act-reflect) plus black-box search engines; there is no RL- or value-learned retrieval policy. The benchmark is designed to evaluate emergent agentic behavior of off-the-shelf LLMs, not to train a retrieval policy.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: No: single-agent, single-framework evaluation with private per-query memory. No memory/experience sharing across multiple agents or heterogeneous frameworks. (The benchmark does compare many different LLMs and search engines plugged into the same unified framework, but they do not share memory.)
benchmarks: InfoDeepSeek (introduced by this paper): 245 human-validated, challenging factual queries for agentic information seeking in the live web, each with >=2 of six difficulty attributes (Multi-Hop 188, Long-Tail 187, Time-Sensitive 162, Freshness 48, Distracting Information 76, False Premise 27), 14 domains, 19 predominant languages, provided in English and Chinese. Comparison table (Table 1) positions it against NQ, MultiHop-RAG, FreshLLM, RGB, CRAG, BrowseComp, and BrowseComp-ZH. Evaluated under the authors' InfoSeekAgents Agentic-RAG framework with four search engines (Google, Bing, Yahoo, DuckDuckGo).
benchmark_family: web / agentic search benchmark (open-web information seeking / Agentic RAG factual QA). Sits in the family of real-world web QA / browsing benchmarks (alongside BrowseComp, BrowseComp-ZH, FreshLLM/FreshQA, CRAG), distinguished by dynamic-environment evaluation rather than a static fixed corpus.
baselines: No prior 'method' baselines (it is a benchmark); instead it benchmarks many LLM agents under a unified framework: Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Instruct, Qwen3-32B (with/without thinking), DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1, GPT-4o, o3-mini, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Gemini-2.5-Pro. It also varies the search-engine backend (Google, Bing, Yahoo, DuckDuckGo) as a controlled factor and contrasts retrieval-augmented vs no-retrieval (parametric-only) behavior (retrieval interference).
key_metrics: Four core metrics: (1) Answer Accuracy (ACC) - LLM-judged correctness of the answer generated from all observations O; (2) Information Accuracy IA@k - correctness of an answer regenerated from only the top-k curated evidence C_{1:k}, a dynamic, gold-document-free measure of evidence quality (utility), reported for k=1..5; (3) Effective Evidence Utilization (EEU) = max_k IA@k / ACC, measuring how well the agent extracts/orders useful evidence (utility); (4) Information Compactness (IC) - evidence-set size relative to the human-annotated supporting-source count |S_q|, with a penalty for answer failures, measuring compactness/redundancy. Accuracy is via LLM-as-judge (DeepSeek-V3 + Gemini-2.0-Flash, GPT-4o-mini/human arbiter), achieving 99.29% agreement with human-eval after false-premise handling.
headline_result: Even SOTA LLMs perform poorly: the best model, Gemini-2.5-Pro, reaches only 22.45% ACC and 21.63% IA@5 under the default DuckDuckGo search engine (T=5, n=5). Search-engine quality dominates: switching Gemini-2.5-Flash from DuckDuckGo (14.29% ACC) to Google raises ACC to 34.29% (IA@3 37.55%), and DeepSeek-V3 jumps from 8.98% (DuckDuckGo) to 28.57% ACC with Google. EEU is mostly below 1 (agents fail to fully exploit retrieved evidence).
ablations: (1) LLM comparison (Table 3): reasoning/search-optimized models lead (DeepSeek-R1 > DeepSeek-V3; o3-mini > GPT-4o; Gemini-2.5-Pro best at 22.45% ACC); IA@k rises then falls with k (later sources add distractors); EEU mostly <1; IC shows large redundancy (~3.7-4.0). (2) Search-engine ablation (Table 4): Google/Yahoo >> Bing > DuckDuckGo; a strong engine partly compensates for a weaker model. (3) Question-attribute breakdown (Fig 3): easier on false-premise/time-sensitive/freshness, hardest on multi-hop/long-tail/distracting-information; reasoning gains concentrate on easy attributes. (4) Test-time scaling (Fig 4): increasing max steps T from 1 to 20 monotonically improves ACC, IA@k, and IC. (5) Retrieval interference (Fig 5a): a measurable fraction of questions answered correctly from parametric knowledge become wrong after noisy retrieval. (6) Language impact (Fig 5b): English > Chinese; predominant-language-aware prompting best. (7) Impact of answer LLM (App D.6) and evaluation-prompt strategy for false premises (95.57% -> 99.29% agreement with humans).
evaluation_decoupling: Yes - a central contribution: intrinsic information-seeking quality (IA@k evidence sufficiency, EEU utilization, IC compactness) is reported separately from end-to-end answer correctness (ACC). Crucially, because the web is dynamic, IA@k replaces static Recall@k/nDCG with a gold-document-free, answer-regeneration-based evidence-quality measure, explicitly decoupling retrieval/augmentation quality from final-answer accuracy.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Both: outcome = ACC (final answer correctness). Process = IA@k (quality/sufficiency of the curated evidence), EEU (how well evidence is utilized/ordered), IC (compactness/redundancy of the seeking process), plus analyses of test-time scaling, retrieval interference, and per-attribute behavior. The framework is explicitly designed to assess the information-seeking process, not just the outcome.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Compute is studied as test-time scaling: varying max retrieval steps T from 1 to 20 trades more search compute for higher ACC/IA@k/IC (clear scaling effect). Information Compactness (IC) directly captures the retrieval-cost-vs-quality tradeoff (over-retrieval is penalized; IC values ~3.3-4.0 indicate substantial redundancy relative to the 1-3 truly needed sources). Default budget: T<=5 steps, evidence set <=5 webpages, ~4,000-char working memory. No dollar/latency/token-count figures are reported per query; dataset construction cost is noted as manual/expensive but not quantified in dollars.
context_budget_and_selection_count: Adaptive, budget-capped selection: the agent dynamically chooses evidence-set size n_q up to a hard cap n=5 (chosen because human-annotated supporting sources |S_q| typically range 1-3), and ranks-then-truncates the candidate webpages by importance. Working memory is capped at ~4,000 characters; retrieval is capped at T<=5 steps by default (ablated 1-20). So selection count is variable but bounded, with reranked-then-truncated context.
benchmark_construction_and_size: Size: 245 high-quality validated queries (HuggingFace InfoDeepSeek_v1), 14 domains, 19 predominant languages (English + Chinese dominant; 17 others incl. Japanese 11, Russian 9, Korean 8, Italian 6, Arabic 6, French 5, etc.), each query >=2 of six difficulty attributes (Multi-Hop 188, Long-Tail 187, Time-Sensitive 162, Freshness 48, Distracting-Info 76, False-Premise 27). Construction: human-curated via reverse construction (start from authoritative/multilingual web knowledge, write a uniquely-answerable question), 'expand from anchor knowledge' (compose long-tail/distracting anchors with extra hops/attributes), and diversification; two filters (determinacy/verifiability check + difficulty filter discarding any question both GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1 solve via single-turn web search); multi-stage validation by two verifiers + a third adjudicator; 7 annotators. Each query stores ground-truth answer y_q, supporting source webpages S_q, and metadata. Answer verifiability: high - deterministic, time-invariant, uniquely-answerable factual answers, scored by LLM-as-judge (99.29% agreement with humans). Difficulty signal: best system (Gemini-2.5-Pro) only 22.45% ACC under DuckDuckGo (and ~34% with Google), confirming the benchmark is hard.
builds_on: Builds on the standard three-stage RAG formulation (retrieval/augmentation/generation; Gao et al. RAG survey, ref 42) extended into Agentic RAG by inserting an autonomous plan-act-reflect LLM agent (ReAct-style planning/reflection). Uses real-world web-QA difficulty notions from FreshLLM/FreshQA, CRAG, RGB, MultiHop-RAG and the browsing-benchmark line BrowseComp / BrowseComp-ZH. Inspired by deployed agentic deep-research products (OpenAI Deep Research, Gemini, Perplexity). Evaluates contemporary LLM agents (GPT-4o, o3-mini, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, DeepSeek-V3/R1, Gemini-2.5-Flash/Pro, Llama-4-Maverick, Qwen3-32B).
contrasts_with: Explicitly contrasts with static, fixed-corpus RAG/QA benchmarks and gold-document retrieval metrics: NQ, TriviaQA, MS MARCO, MultiHop-RAG, RGB, CRAG, FreshLLM/FreshQA (Table 1). Versus real-web browsing benchmarks BrowseComp and BrowseComp-ZH, InfoDeepSeek adds dynamic-environment information-seeking evaluation (Dyna.Eval.), LLM-based difficulty filtering, and the full set of six difficulty attributes (freshness, time-sensitivity, distracting info, false premise) that those lack. It contrasts gold-set Recall@k/nDCG (infeasible in dynamic web) with its IA@k / EEU / IC framework.
lineage: Surveys/benchmarks line (evaluation infrastructure for retrieval-augmented agents): a benchmark + evaluation-framework contribution for Agentic RAG / agentic information seeking. It extends the RAG-benchmark lineage (NQ/TriviaQA -> RGB/CRAG/MultiHop-RAG/FreshQA -> BrowseComp/BrowseComp-ZH) into dynamic open-web, agent-driven, gold-document-free evaluation, and provides process-level metrics (IA@k/EEU/IC) for the retrieval+augmentation stages of agentic RAG systems.
cbr_cycle_coverage: N/A: not a case-based-reasoning system. No Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain over a case library; retrieval targets the live web, not prior solved cases.
explicit_cbr_grounding: False: the paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is an Agentic RAG information-seeking benchmark.
tool_document_engineering: N/A: the agent's tools (search engines, Selenium browser, time utility, termination) are exposed via a tool_specification in the prompt, but the benchmark does not engineer/index tool documentation for retrieval (tools are few and fixed, selected by the LLM during planning, not retrieved by similarity).
index_content_separation: Partial / implicit: search returns lightweight snippets/titles first, and the agent uses the Selenium browser to fetch heavier full webpage content on demand (progressive disclosure from snippet to full page). This is a property of the web/search backend rather than a designed lightweight-index-then-content store built by the benchmark.
dynamic_index_and_protocol: Live/dynamic external retrieval over real search-engine and browser tools: Google (via Serper API), Bing and Yahoo (via SerpApi), DuckDuckGo (free API with Selenium fallback), plus a Selenium-based live-webpage browser and a time utility. Integration is via each engine's API with Selenium scraping fallback; supports OpenAI/Gemini/DeepSeek/Qwen LLM clients. Not MCP; not a synchronized tool index with CRUD - the 'index' is the live web itself, queried in real time.
tool_dependency_awareness: N/A: with only a small fixed toolset (search engines, browser, time tool, terminate), the benchmark does not model inter-tool dependencies, dependency graphs, or dependency-aware tool reranking; tool sequencing is left to the LLM's step-by-step planning.
adaptation_mechanism: N/A (not CBR): no retrieved-case adaptation. The closest analogue is the augmentation stage's LLM-based selection, summarization, and importance ranking of retrieved web evidence, plus iterative replanning/reflection over the trajectory - but this adapts a search strategy to observations, not a prior solved case to a new problem.
